lesson.title: Property, Not Citizens: The Dred Scott Decision
lesson.summary: In 1857 the Supreme Court ruled that Black Americans could never be citizens and struck down the Missouri Compromise, a decision meant to settle the slavery question that instead pushed the nation closer to war.
lesson.body:
Dred Scott was an enslaved man owned by a United States Army surgeon named John Emerson. In the 1830s, Emerson's military postings took Scott to Illinois, a free state, and then to Fort Snelling in the Wisconsin Territory, land where slavery was banned under the Missouri Compromise line of 1820. When Scott and his owner eventually returned to the slave state of Missouri, Scott sued for his freedom in Missouri courts in 1846, arguing that his years of residence on free soil had legally made him a free man. After years of appeals, his case reached the United States Supreme Court as Dred Scott v. Sandford, decided in March 1857.

Chief Justice Roger B. Taney wrote the majority opinion for a Supreme Court that ruled seven to two against Scott, and the decision went far beyond the narrow question of his personal freedom. Taney held that Black Americans, whether enslaved or free, were not and never could be citizens of the United States, meaning Scott had no legal standing to bring a lawsuit in federal court at all. The opinion described Black Americans as having essentially no legal claims that white citizens were bound to honor, language that shocked even many northerners who had not previously counted themselves strong opponents of slavery.

Taney did not stop there. Having already ruled that Scott could not sue, the Court went on to rule that Congress had never possessed the constitutional power to ban slavery in the federal territories in the first place, which meant the Missouri Compromise line of 1820 had been unconstitutional from the moment it was written. This was only the second time in American history that the Supreme Court had struck down an act of Congress, the first being Marbury v. Madison back in 1803, and it showed how far the power of judicial review, once used sparingly, could reach into the nation's most explosive political question.

The ruling also created an unexpected problem for Stephen Douglas and his doctrine of popular sovereignty. If Congress itself had no power to keep slavery out of a territory, it was hard to explain how a mere territorial legislature, a body with less authority than Congress, could have that power either. Douglas would be forced to grapple with this contradiction directly during his 1858 Senate campaign against Abraham Lincoln, since northern and southern Democrats read the implications of Dred Scott very differently.

Reaction split sharply along sectional lines. Republicans and other northerners saw the decision as proof that a slaveholding minority had captured not just Congress and the presidency but the Supreme Court as well, and the ruling energized the young Republican Party's argument that slavery's power was actively expanding rather than merely persisting where it already existed. Southerners largely celebrated the decision as a vindication of their constitutional position. Dred Scott himself gained personal freedom only months later, in May 1857, when his case's original owners arranged to purchase and then free him and his family, but he died of tuberculosis the following year, never seeing the broader legal principles of his case swept away by the constitutional amendments that followed the Civil War.
